name: Restore the Permutation
description: A sequence of $$$n$$$ numbers is called permutation if it contains all numbers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ exactly once. For example, the sequences [$$$3, 1, 4, 2$$$], [$$$1$$$] and [$$$2,1$$$] are permutations, but [$$$1,2,1$$$], [$$$0,1$$$] and [$$$1,3,4$$$] — are not. For a permutation $$$p$$$ of even length $$$n$$$ you can make an array $$$b$$$ of length $$$\frac{n}{2}$$$ such that: $$$b_i = \max(p_{2i - 1}, p_{2i})$$$ for $$$1 \le i \le \frac{n}{2}$$$ For example, if $$$p$$$ = [$$$2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 6$$$], then: $$$b_1 = \max(p_1, p_2) = \max(2, 4) = 4$$$ $$$b_2 = \max(p_3, p_4) = \max(3,1)=3$$$ $$$b_3 = \max(p_5, p_6) = \max(5,6) = 6$$$ As a result, we made $$$b$$$ = $$$[4, 3, 6]$$$. For a given array $$$b$$$, find the lexicographically minimal permutation $$$p$$$ such that you can make the given array $$$b$$$ from it. If $$$b$$$ = [$$$4,3,6$$$], then the lexicographically minimal permutation from which it can be made is $$$p$$$ = [$$$1,4,2,3,5,6$$$], since: $$$b_1 = \max(p_1, p_2) = \max(1, 4) = 4$$$ $$$b_2 = \max(p_3, p_4) = \max(2, 3) = 3$$$ $$$b_3 = \max(p_5, p_6) = \max(5, 6) = 6$$$ A permutation $$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$$$ is lexicographically smaller than a permutation $$$y_1, y_2 \dots, y_n$$$ if and only if there exists such $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$) that $$$x_1=y_1, x_2=y_2, \dots, x_{i-1}=y_{i-1}$$$ and $$$x_i \lt y_i$$$.
input_specification: The first line of input data contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains one even integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$). The second line of each test case contains exactly $$$\frac{n}{2}$$$ integers $$$b_i$$$ ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$) — elements of array $$$b$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ values over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print on a separate line: lexicographically minimal permutation $$$p$$$ such that you can make an array $$$b$$$ from it; or a number -1 if the permutation you are looking for does not exist.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1759G — Restore the Permutation [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
